title: Variables and quoting
goal: Use variables, quotes, command substitution and arithmetic correctly, and know which variables a child process can see.
setup: # P2: version file of the backend
# P3: a child script that reads two variables
# P4: a script that shows special variables

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' 'echo "script name (\$0): $0"' 'echo "first arg  (\$1): $1"' 'echo "arg count  (\$#): $#"' 'echo "all args   (\$@): $@"' 'echo "my PID     (\$\$): $$"' 'false' 'echo "last exit  (\$?): $?"' > args.sh
# P5: a project folder with a space in its name, and a broken backup script
# P6: a small tool for the PATH problem
# P7: a demo settings file (NOT your real ~/.bashrc)
printf '%s\n' 'export GREETING="hello from demo-bashrc"' 'alias ll="ls -l"' > demo-bashrc

warmup.q: Which redirect saves stdout and stderr of `job.sh` in `job.log`?

warmup.a: The redirect is done by the normal user's shell, not by sudo. Use `echo x | sudo tee -a /etc/file`.

warmup.q: Which grep option shows lines that do NOT match?
Does root care about a file permission of 600?
warmup.a: No. Root ignores read and write permissions. 600 only blocks other normal users.

problems.title: Predict: single quotes, double quotes, no quotes
problems.situation: A deploy message printed `Deploying $APP` instead of the app name. Another script broke on a folder name with a space. Quotes decide what bash does with `$`, spaces and wildcards.
task: Set `APP=todo-api` and `DIR="my project"`. (No spaces around `=`!)
Predict, then run: `echo "Deploying $APP"` and `echo 'Deploying $APP'`.
Predict, then run: `echo "Path: ~/$APP"` and `echo Path: ~/$APP`.
Predict, then run: `ls $DIR` and `ls "$DIR"`.
Predict, then run: `echo "Today is $(date +%A)" | wc -w` (the day name changes, the count does not).
hints: Double quotes: `$var` and `$(cmd)` are replaced, but spaces stay inside one word.
Single quotes: nothing is replaced. The text is printed exactly.
Without quotes, `$DIR` is split at the space into two words: `my` and `project`.
solution: echo 'Deploying $APP'        # single quotes: printed as written
echo "Path: ~/$APP"          # ~ is NOT expanded inside quotes
ls $DIR || echo "exit code: $?"   # split into 'my' and 'project'

explanation.meaning: Double quotes: variables and `$( )` are replaced. Spaces stay in one argument.
Single quotes: no replacement at all. Good for literal `$` text, regex and awk code.
The tilde `~` becomes the home folder only when it is not quoted. In scripts, use `$HOME`.
No quotes: bash splits the value at spaces. `ls` gets two names that do not exist.
Command substitution: run the command and put its output here.

problems.expected_output:
Deploying todo-api
Deploying $APP
Path: ~/todo-api
Path: /home/wicky/todo-api
ls: cannot access 'my': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access 'project': No such file or directory
exit code: 2
README.md
3
mistakes: Spaces around `=`: `APP = todo-api` gives `bash: APP: command not found`. Bash thinks `APP` is a command.
Single quotes around a variable in a message: `echo 'Hello $USER'` prints `Hello $USER`.
Not quoting a path with spaces: `ls: cannot access 'my': No such file or directory`.
problems.interview_say: Double quotes expand variables but keep spaces together; single quotes keep everything literal. I quote every variable, like `"$DIR"`, so spaces in names do not break my scripts.
problems.try_yourself: Run `echo "$APP"s` and `echo "${APP}s"` and `echo "$APPs"`. Why is the last one empty?

problems.title: Build a release tag with $( ) and $(( ))
problems.situation: The CI pipeline needs a tag like `todo-api-2.4.1-build8` for the Docker image, plus an error rate for the release notes. The version is in a file, and the build number is the last build plus one.
task: Read the version from the file `VERSION` into a variable with `$(cat VERSION)`.
Set `LAST_BUILD=7`, and compute `BUILD=$((LAST_BUILD + 1))`.
Print the tag `todo-api-<version>-build<number>`. Use `${VERSION}` in braces.
Count all lines and the `500` lines of `access.log` with `$( )`.
Print the error rate in percent with `$(( ))` (whole numbers only).
hints: `VAR=$(command)` saves the output of a command.
Inside `$(( ))` variables need no `$`: `$((a + 1))` works.
Bash arithmetic is integer only: `$((ERRORS * 100 / TOTAL))` gives 25, not 25.0.

explanation.meaning: Command substitution: the file content becomes the value.
Arithmetic expansion: whole-number math. No `$` needed inside.
Braces mark where the variable name ends, so text can follow directly.
With `<` wc prints only the number (no file name), good for variables.
`$` at the end of a regex = end of the line. So only the status code at the end matches.
Integer division and remainder. For decimals use `awk` or `bc` (Day 11).

problems.expected_output:
Image tag: todo-api-2.4.1-build8
Requests: 4, errors: 1
Error rate: 25%
7 / 2 in bash is 3, remainder 1
mistakes: Old backticks `` `cat VERSION` `` work but are hard to read and to nest. Use `$( )`.
Writing `$(LAST_BUILD + 1)` with one pair of brackets: bash tries to run a command called `LAST_BUILD`: `bash: LAST_BUILD: command not found`.
problems.interview_say: I use `$(command)` to save command output in a variable and `$(( ))` for integer math, for example to compute a build number or a percentage.
problems.try_yourself: Compute the percentage with one decimal using awk: `awk -v e="$ERRORS" -v t="$TOTAL" 'BEGIN { printf "%.1f\n", e*100/t }'`.

problems.title: export: why the child script sees nothing
problems.situation: The user sets `DB_HOST` in the terminal and starts the backend with a script, but the script says `DB_HOST` is empty. Only exported variables are passed to child processes (programs started from this shell).
task: Set `DB_HOST=db.internal` (no export) and run `./child.sh`.
Now `export DB_HOST` and run `./child.sh` again.
Give `LOG_LEVEL=debug` only to one run: `LOG_LEVEL=debug ./child.sh`. Then run `./child.sh` once more.
Check the environment with `printenv DB_HOST` and `env | grep '^DB_'`.
Remove the variable with `unset DB_HOST` and run `./child.sh`.
hints: A normal variable lives only in the current shell. `export` puts it into the environment.
`NAME=value command` sets the variable only for that one command.
`printenv NAME` prints one environment variable; `env` prints all of them.
solution: ./child.sh                       # not exported: the child sees nothing
LOG_LEVEL=debug ./child.sh       # only for this one command

explanation.meaning: A shell variable. Only this shell can see it.
Mark it as an environment variable. Every child process gets a copy.
Set a variable for one command only. Common for one-time settings.
Show environment variables (only exported ones).
Delete a variable.

problems.expected_output:
child sees DB_HOST=[] LOG_LEVEL=[]
child sees DB_HOST=[db.internal] LOG_LEVEL=[]
child sees DB_HOST=[db.internal] LOG_LEVEL=[debug]
child sees DB_HOST=[db.internal] LOG_LEVEL=[]
db.internal
DB_HOST=db.internal
child sees DB_HOST=[] LOG_LEVEL=[]
mistakes: Expecting a child to change the parent: a script that runs `export X=1` does not change the terminal that started it. Use `source script.sh` for that.
Writing `export $DB_HOST`. That exports a variable with the name `db.internal`. Write `export DB_HOST` (no `$`).
problems.interview_say: Only exported variables go to child processes. In Docker and Kubernetes, settings reach the app the same way: as environment variables.
problems.try_yourself: Run `bash -c 'echo $DB_HOST'` before and after `export`. `bash -c` is also a child process.

problems.title: Special variables: $0 $1 $# $@ $? $$
problems.situation: A deploy script must check its arguments: how many were given, what the first one is, and whether the last command worked. Bash fills special variables for this.
task: Read `args.sh` with `cat args.sh`.
Run `./args.sh staging "todo api" v2`. Look at each line.
Run it with no arguments: `./args.sh`.
Run `ls /nope; echo "exit: $?"` and `ls /tmp > /dev/null; echo "exit: $?"`.
hints: `$1` is the first argument, `$#` the number of arguments, `$@` all arguments.
`$?` is the exit code of the **last** command. Read it right away; the next command changes it.
`$$` is the process ID of the shell running the script. It changes every run.

explanation.meaning: The name the script was started with.
Positional parameters: the arguments in order. `"todo api"` is one argument because of the quotes.
How many arguments.
All arguments. Write it as `"$@"` to keep each one separate (Day 9).
PID of the current shell. Useful for unique temp file names.
Exit code of the last command: 0 = success, other = error.

problems.expected_output:
#!/bin/bash
echo "script name (\$0): $0"
echo "first arg  (\$1): $1"
echo "arg count  (\$#): $#"
echo "all args   (\$@): $@"
echo "my PID     (\$\$): $$"
false
echo "last exit  (\$?): $?"
script name ($0): ./args.sh
first arg  ($1): staging
arg count  ($#): 3
all args   ($@): staging todo api v2
my PID     ($$): 25682
last exit  ($?): 1
--- no arguments ---
script name ($0): ./args.sh
first arg  ($1):
arg count  ($#): 0
all args   ($@):
my PID     ($$): 25683
last exit  ($?): 1
ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory
exit: 2
exit: 0
problems.output_note: The PID (`$$`) is different on every run. The `ls` error text is the same on the user's machine.
mistakes: Running another command before reading `$?`: then `$?` belongs to that command (often `echo`, which is 0).
Using `$10` for the tenth argument. Bash reads it as `$1` followed by `0`. Write `${10}`.
problems.interview_say: `$1` and so on are the arguments, `$#` their number, `$@` all of them, `$?` the last exit code and `$$` the PID. I check `$#` at the start of a script and print a usage message if it is wrong.
problems.try_yourself: Run `./args.sh a b c d e f g h i j` and add a line `echo "${10}"` to the script. What prints?

problems.title: Find the bug: the backup script variables
problems.situation: `backup.sh` should copy the folder `my project` into `backups/<user name>/`. It prints strange errors, and a folder named `$USER` appears.
task: Read and run `bash backup.sh`. Read every error.
Run `ls backups` (if it exists). Is the folder name correct?
Find 3 bugs about `=`, quotes and spaces. Fix them.
Delete the wrong folder: `rm -rf 'backups/$USER'` (single quotes, so the name is exact). Run the fixed script.
Check with `ls -R backups`.
hints: Line 2: look at the spaces.
Line 3: which quotes stop `$USER` from being replaced?
Line 5: the folder name has a space. Quote the variable.
solution: rm -rf 'backups/$USER'           # remove the folder with the literal name $USER
cp -r "$SRC" "$DEST"/            # quotes keep "my project" as one name

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: spaces around `=`. Bash ran a command `SRC`: `SRC: command not found`.
Bug 2: single quotes. The folder was really named `$USER`.
Bug 3: no quotes. With the right value, `my project` is split into `my` and `project`.
Single quotes so `rm` gets the literal name, not `backups/wicky`.

problems.expected_output:
backup.sh: line 2: SRC: command not found
cp: missing destination file operand after 'backups/$USER/'
Try 'cp --help' for more information.
Saved  to backups/$USER
Saved my project to backups/wicky
backups:
wicky

backups/wicky:
'my project'

'backups/wicky/my project':
README.md
problems.output_note: The folder name is the user name. On the learner's WSL it is `wicky`, like here.
mistakes: Fixing bug 1 but not bug 3: then `cp: cannot stat 'my': No such file or directory`.
Deleting with `rm -rf backups/$USER` (no quotes): this deletes `backups/wicky`, not the wrong folder.

checks.run: SRC="my project"; mkdir -p out; cp -r $SRC out/
checks.expect: cp: cannot stat 'my': No such file or directory

problems.interview_say: Most bash bugs I see are quoting bugs: spaces around `=`, single quotes that stop a variable, and unquoted paths with spaces. ShellCheck finds all three.
problems.try_yourself: If ShellCheck is installed (`sudo apt install -y shellcheck`), run `shellcheck backup.sh` on the broken version. Read the codes, like SC2086.

problems.title: PATH: run your own tool by name
problems.situation: The team has small helper scripts in `~/bash-practice/day05/bin`. The user wants to type `todo-status` from any folder, like a normal command. Bash finds commands by searching the folders in `PATH`.
task: Try `todo-status`. Read the error.
Show the first 3 folders in PATH: `echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | head -n 3`.
Add the folder at the front: `export PATH="$HOME/bash-practice/day05/bin:$PATH"`.
Run `todo-status` again and check where it comes from with `command -v todo-status`.
hints: PATH is a list of folders separated by `:`.
Keep the old value: always include `:$PATH` when adding a folder.
To keep it after closing the terminal, add the export line to `~/.bashrc`.

explanation.meaning: Bash searched every PATH folder and found nothing. Exit code 127.
Replace each `:` with a new line, so each folder is on its own line.
Put the new folder first, keep all old folders after it.
Show which file bash will run for a name.

problems.expected_output:
bash: todo-status: command not found
exit code: 127
/usr/local/sbin
/usr/local/bin
/usr/sbin
todo-api: running (version 2.4.1)
/home/wicky/bash-practice/day05/bin/todo-status
problems.output_note: The user's real PATH is longer. On WSL it also contains many Windows folders like `/mnt/c/Windows`.
mistakes: `export PATH="$HOME/bin"` without `:$PATH`. Now `ls` and `grep` are not found: `ls: command not found`. Open a new terminal to fix it.
Using `~` inside quotes: `"~/bin:$PATH"`. The `~` is not expanded. Use `$HOME`.
problems.interview_say: PATH is a colon-separated list of folders where bash looks for commands. I add a folder with `export PATH="/my/bin:$PATH"` and make it permanent in `~/.bashrc`.
problems.try_yourself: Run `type ls cd todo-status`. `type` shows if a name is a program, an alias or a shell builtin.

problems.title: source vs run, and .bashrc vs .profile
problems.situation: The user adds `export GREETING=...` to a settings file and runs it, but the variable is still empty. Running a file starts a child shell; `source` reads the file into the current shell. Here we use `demo-bashrc`, not the real `~/.bashrc`.
task: Read `demo-bashrc`.
Run it as a script: `bash demo-bashrc`, then `echo "[$GREETING]"`.
Load it with `source demo-bashrc` (or `. demo-bashrc`), then `echo "[$GREETING]"`.
Read the table: which file runs when?
hints: `bash file` = new child shell. Its variables are gone when it ends.
`source file` = run the lines in this shell.
After editing `~/.bashrc`, run `source ~/.bashrc` to load it without opening a new terminal.

explanation.meaning: Runs in a child shell. The export happens there and disappears.
Runs the lines in the current shell, so the variable stays.
Same as `source` (POSIX short form).

problems.expected_output:
export GREETING="hello from demo-bashrc"
alias ll="ls -l"
after bash:   []
after source: [hello from demo-bashrc]
problems.output_note: On Ubuntu, `~/.profile` also loads `~/.bashrc`, so on WSL both run when a terminal opens.
mistakes: Editing `~/.bashrc` and expecting the open terminal to change. Run `source ~/.bashrc` or open a new terminal.
Putting `echo` lines in `~/.bashrc`: they can break `scp` and other tools that start bash without a terminal.
problems.interview_say: `~/.bashrc` runs for every interactive shell, so I put aliases there. `~/.profile` runs at login, so I put PATH and environment variables there. To reload a file I use `source`.
problems.try_yourself: After `source demo-bashrc`, run `ll`. The alias works. Then run `bash -c 'll'`. Why does it fail?

interview.q: What is the difference between single and double quotes in bash?
interview.a: Double quotes replace variables and `$( )`, but keep spaces in one word. Single quotes print everything exactly, with no replacement.
It puts a variable into the environment, so child processes (scripts and programs started from this shell) can see it.
The exit code of the last command. 0 means success; any other number means an error.
A colon-separated list of folders. Bash searches these folders, in order, when the user types a command name.

interview.q: What is the difference between `$(command)` and `$((1 + 2))`?
interview.a: `$(command)` runs a command and uses its output. `$(( ))` does integer arithmetic.
